content: Individuals with cystic fibrosis are at a heightened risk of developing deficiencies in fat-soluble vitamins, including vitamin E. A deficiency in vitamin E can result in several serious health conditions, such as hemolytic anemia, cerebellar ataxia, and cognitive impairments. To address this, vitamin E supplementation is commonly recommended for individuals with cystic fibrosis to mitigate these deficiencies. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of vitamin E supplementation, at any dosage or duration, on the occurrence of vitamin E deficiency-related disorders in people with cystic fibrosis. The review included randomized controlled trials and quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared any form of vitamin E supplementation to either a placebo or no supplementation. The evidence was gathered from the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis Trials Register and international online trial registries, with the most recent searches conducted in August and July 2020, respectively. Four studies involving a total of 141 participants were included in the review. Two of these studies focused on children aged six months to 14.5 years, while the other two did not specify the participants' ages. The studies utilized various formulations and doses of vitamin E, with treatment durations ranging from 10 days to six months. Two studies compared fat-soluble and water-soluble vitamin E formulations to no supplementation, one study compared a water-soluble formulation to a placebo, and another study assessed a fat-soluble formulation against a placebo. The quality of the evidence was compromised due to limited details regarding randomization and blinding in the included studies. Additionally, the variability in the formulations and their differing bioavailabilities reduced the generalizability of the findings to the broader cystic fibrosis population. None of the studies reported on the primary outcomes of the review, such as the vitamin E total lipid ratio or the incidence of vitamin E-specific deficiency disorders. Secondary outcomes, including lung function and quality of life, were also not reported. For water-soluble vitamin E, one study with 45 participants demonstrated an improvement in serum vitamin E levels at six months, with a mean difference (MD) of 19.74 µmol/L (95% confidence interval [CI] 13.48 to 26.00). Similar improvements were observed at one month (MD 17.66 µmol/L, 95% CI 10.59 to 24.74) and three months (MD 11.61 µmol/L, 95% CI 4.77 to 18.45) in smaller studies. However, only one study reported on weight as a secondary outcome, and no differences were observed between the treatment and control groups at one or six months. For fat-soluble vitamin E, two studies with 36 participants reported higher serum vitamin E levels at one month compared to controls (MD 13.59 µmol/L, 95% CI 9.52 to 17.66). However, at three months, one study found no significant difference between the treatment and control groups. None of the studies in this comparison reported on growth or nutritional status. In conclusion, vitamin E supplementation may improve serum vitamin E levels in individuals with cystic fibrosis, but the quality of the evidence is low. There is insufficient data to draw conclusions about other potential benefits, such as improvements in lung function, growth, or quality of life. Future research should focus on larger, well-designed studies, particularly in individuals already receiving pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy and vitamin E supplementation. These studies should aim to evaluate specific outcomes, including vitamin E status, lung function, nutritional status, and the optimal dosage required for maximum clinical benefit.
